front.title: A Selection Algorithm for Concurrent TCP Option (SEG-U and SEG-O) Size Requests

abstract.t: defines an Upgraded TCP Segment (SEG-U) which can carry up to 1016 octets of TCP options, by setting the Data Offset field to 0, and introducing a "length" field. Given that the TCP-U is designed to be backwards compatible with TCP-O, hosts which supports this new TCP-U, are expected to support both segment formats, SEG-U and SEG-O. So, there is a chance, that during connection setup, the host receive requests for either. When such requests arrive concurrently (or successively), for what would otherwise be the same session, the host must decide which format to accept and which to decline.

This document defines an algorithm for dual-capable hosts to select between a TCP-U and a TCP-O when presented with both. It specifies selection inputs, tie-breaking, fallback behaviour, and the interaction with the existing TCP state machine.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The Upgraded TCP Segment (SEG-U) format defined in raises the TCP options ceiling from 40 octets to 1016 octets by repurposing the Data Offset field: A value of zero marks a segment as SEG-U rather than classic TCP (SEG-O). Legacy stacks reject dataofs < 5 and therefore drop SEG-U silently, giving the format implicit backwards compatibility.

Hosts that implements both SEG-U and SEG-O can, in the course of normal operation, be offered either kind of session. In some deployments the same peer (or two peers acting on behalf of the same application) may present both a SEG-U and a SEG-O initiation for what the host would treat as a single session. Without a procedure, the outcome is implementation-dependent and may vary between stacks, defeating the interoperability goals of .

This document specifies a deterministic selection algorithm for such hosts. It does not change the SEG-U or SEG-O wire formats and does not alter the classic TCP three-way handshake beyond the point at which the host commits to one format or the other.
